title: Joining Ideas
overview: Level 1 gave you because and so, which join a reason to a result. This unit gives you the rest of the system, and the practical difficulty is not meaning but punctuation: three groups of connectors mean similar things and attach to sentences in three different ways. Getting that wrong produces the most common punctuation error in English writing. It ends with a paragraph rewritten three times, because connectors are where writing stops being a list of sentences.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 2 is where the punctuation goes wrong for almost everybody.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is one paragraph written three ways.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the diagnostic — the comma splice.
Record yourself arguing one point for two minutes.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
In Level 1 Unit 13 you learned because and so. Because gives a reason, so gives a result, and Unit 18 added so that for purpose. That is enough for speech. It is not enough for writing, and this unit fills the gap.
The difficulty here is not meaning. Most of these words are easy to understand when you read them. The difficulty is that they attach to sentences in three different ways, and using the wrong attachment produces an error that is very common and very visible.
So I am going to organise this by how the word attaches, not by what it means.
Group one: subordinating conjunctions. These join two clauses into one sentence.
Because, although, while, whereas, since, as, unless, if, when, after, before, until.
They work like because, which you already have. Two clauses, one sentence, and the conjunction can go in the middle or at the front.
Although it was raining, we went. We went although it was raining.
Both correct. When the clause comes first, it takes a comma. When it comes second, usually no comma.
And there is one rule about these that catches learners from many language backgrounds. English uses one connector per relationship, not two.
Although it was raining, but we went — that is wrong. You have although and but doing the same job. Choose one.
This is the same error as because and so together, which Unit 13 warned about. English marks the relationship once.
Group two: connective adverbs. However, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, consequently, furthermore, thus, instead, otherwise.
These do not join clauses. They are adverbs — they belong to a sentence and comment on its relationship to the previous one.
And this is where the punctuation error lives.
It was raining, however we went. That is wrong.
It was raining. However, we went. That is right.
Or: It was raining; however, we went.
However cannot join two sentences with a comma, because it is not a conjunction. It is an adverb sitting inside the second sentence.
The error has a name — the comma splice — and it is the most common punctuation error in English writing, made constantly by first-language writers as well.
The test that fixes it: can the word be moved inside its clause?
However, we went. We, however, went. We went, however. All three work, because however is an adverb and adverbs move.
Now try but. But we went. We but went. We went but. Only the first works, because but is a conjunction and conjunctions are fixed at the join.
So: if the word can move, it is an adverb, and it needs a full stop or a semicolon before it. If it cannot move, it is a conjunction, and a comma is fine.
That test is worth more than memorising which words are in which group.
Group three: prepositions. Despite, in spite of, because of, owing to.
These take a noun, not a clause.
Despite the rain, we went. Not despite it was raining.
If you want a clause after despite, you have to add the fact that: despite the fact that it was raining. That is correct and heavy, and usually the better move is to switch to although.
So you have three ways to express contrast and they attach differently.
Although it was raining, we went. Conjunction, one sentence.
It was raining. However, we went. Adverb, two sentences.
Despite the rain, we went. Preposition, takes a noun.
Same idea, three structures, and the structure decides the punctuation.
Third pattern: although, while and whereas specifically, because they are not interchangeable.
Although is concession. It means this is true, and the other thing is true anyway. Although it was raining, we went.
Whereas is comparison. It sets two different things side by side, and there is no concession at all. The first site uses the old system, whereas the second has moved to the new one. Neither is surprising; they are just different.
While does both, which is why it is confusing. While it was raining, we went — concession. The first site uses the old system, while the second has moved — comparison. And while also means during, which is the meaning you will meet in Unit 11 with past tenses.
So while is ambiguous and the other two are not. In careful writing, use although for concession and whereas for comparison, and reserve while for time. That is a style recommendation rather than a rule, and it will make your writing clearer than most.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: In addition; and there is more.
words.example: The cost is high. Furthermore, it is not fixed.
practice: It is late; furthermore, it is incomplete.
The delay is one problem. Furthermore, so is the cost.
words.starter: The cost is high. Furthermore, it is not
words.tutor: Furthermore is an adverb. Say it after a full stop, never after a comma.

words.meaning: In addition, and often more importantly.
words.example: It is expensive. Moreover, it does not solve the problem.
practice: It is slow; moreover, it is unreliable.
words.starter: It is expensive. Moreover, it does not solve the
words.tutor: Moreover often introduces the stronger of two points. Say two points with it.

words.meaning: In addition; and anyway.
words.example: It is too late. Besides, nobody wants it.
practice: Besides, it would cost too much.
I do not want to; besides, I cannot.
words.starter: It is too late. Besides, nobody wants
words.tutor: Besides is less formal than furthermore. Say where you would use each.

words.meaning: As an extra point.
words.example: Additionally, the site has no parking.
practice: It is small; additionally, it is dark.
words.starter: Additionally, the site has no
words.tutor: Additionally is quite formal. Say it in a report sentence.

words.meaning: In the same way; the same is true of.
words.example: The first site failed. Likewise, the second.
practice: Likewise, the older machines were affected.
She agreed; likewise, so did the others.
The result was the same. Likewise the cause.
words.starter: The first site failed. Likewise, the
words.tutor: Likewise means the same applies. Say two similar facts joined by it.

words.meaning: In a similar way.
words.example: Similarly, the second report reaches the wrong conclusion.
practice: The first failed; similarly, the second.
words.starter: Similarly, the second report reaches the wrong
words.tutor: Say similarly and likewise. They are close; similarly is slightly softer.

words.meaning: But; on the other hand. An adverb, not a conjunction.
words.example: It was raining. However, we went.
practice: It is cheap; however, it is slow.
We went, however, without much hope.
words.starter: It was raining. However, we
words.tutor: Say however, we went and we, however, went. It moves, so it is an adverb.

words.meaning: In spite of that.
words.example: The evidence is thin. Nevertheless, the conclusion may be right.
practice: It failed; nevertheless, it was worth trying.
Nevertheless, I would do it again.
words.starter: The evidence is thin. Nevertheless, the conclusion may be
words.tutor: Nevertheless concedes and then continues. Say a concession followed by it.

words.meaning: In spite of that. Almost identical to nevertheless.
words.example: It is expensive. Nonetheless, it is the best option.
practice: It is slow; nonetheless, it works.
words.starter: It is expensive. Nonetheless, it is the best
words.tutor: Nonetheless and nevertheless are interchangeable. Say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: In the opposite way.
words.example: The first site is overstaffed. Conversely, the second is short.
practice: Conversely, the cheaper option lasted longer.
Conversely, the older system is more reliable.
words.starter: The first site is overstaffed. Conversely, the second is
words.tutor: Conversely marks an opposite, not just a difference. Say when whereas would fit better.

words.meaning: In spite of. Takes a noun, not a clause.
words.example: Despite the rain, we went.
practice: Despite the cost, it was worth it.
Despite the delay, we finished on time.
Despite the fact that it was raining, we went.
words.starter: Despite the rain, we
words.tutor: Despite takes a noun. Say despite the rain, never despite it was raining.

words.meaning: Without paying attention to the situation; anyway.
words.example: The deadline stands regardless.
practice: Regardless of the cost, it has to be done.
Regardless of what happens, tell me.
It applies regardless of the reason.
words.starter: The deadline stands
words.tutor: Say regardless of something. It works like despite when it takes of.

words.meaning: For that reason.
words.example: The evidence is incomplete. Therefore, no conclusion is possible.
practice: It failed twice; therefore, it was replaced.
The cost has risen; we must therefore reconsider.
words.starter: The evidence is incomplete. Therefore, no conclusion is
words.tutor: Therefore is the formal version of so. Say the same sentence with each.

words.meaning: As a result; in this way. Formal.
words.example: The seal had failed and thus water entered.
practice: Thus the problem was not detected.
It was never checked; thus nothing was found.
Thus we arrive at the same conclusion.
words.starter: The seal had failed and thus water
words.tutor: Thus is more formal than therefore and often takes no comma. Say one sentence.

words.meaning: For this reason. Formal, and often followed by a noun phrase.
words.example: The route was closed, hence the delay.
practice: Nobody was informed, hence the confusion.
The system is old, hence the failures.
words.starter: The route was closed, hence the
words.tutor: Hence often introduces a noun rather than a clause. Say hence the delay.

words.meaning: As a result.
words.example: Nothing was recorded. Consequently, nobody knew.
practice: It was late; consequently, we missed the connection.
words.starter: Nothing was recorded. Consequently, nobody
words.tutor: Consequently is the adverb version of so. Say it after a full stop.

words.meaning: In a way that fits what has been said; therefore.
words.example: The rules have changed. Accordingly, the form has been reissued.
practice: Accordingly, no further action is needed.
We have adjusted the schedule accordingly.
words.starter: The rules have changed. Accordingly, the form has been
words.tutor: Accordingly also works at the end: plan accordingly. Say it both ways.

words.meaning: Considering everything together.
words.example: Overall, the change has been positive.
words.starter: Overall, the change has been
words.tutor: Overall introduces a summary judgement. Say it at the start of a conclusion.

words.meaning: As the first point.
words.example: Firstly, the cost is higher than stated.
practice: Firstly, and most importantly, it is late.
Firstly, let me deal with the cost.
words.starter: Firstly, the cost is higher than
words.tutor: Say firstly and first. Both are used; firstly is slightly more formal.

words.meaning: At the beginning, before things changed.
words.example: Initially the plan was different.
words.starter: Initially the plan was
words.tutor: Initially sets up a change. Say initially, then say what happened later.

words.meaning: Afterwards; following that.
words.example: The seal was replaced. Subsequently the fault returned.
words.starter: The seal was replaced. Subsequently the fault
words.tutor: Subsequently is the formal version of then. Say the same sentence with each.

words.meaning: In the end; when everything is considered.
words.example: Ultimately, the decision is not ours.
words.starter: Ultimately, the decision is not
words.tutor: Ultimately introduces the final consideration. Say it before a conclusion.

words.meaning: After that time.
words.example: Notice is one week for the first three months and four weeks thereafter.
practice: It was free for a year and chargeable thereafter.
words.starter: Notice is one week for the first three months and four weeks
words.tutor: Thereafter appears constantly in contracts. Say a two-stage rule using it.

words.meaning: As the final point.
words.example: Lastly, there is the question of cost.
practice: Lastly, I would add one thing.
words.starter: Lastly, there is the question of
words.tutor: Say firstly and lastly to open and close a list of points.

words.meaning: It is true that; conceding a point.
words.example: Admittedly the evidence is thin.
words.starter: Admittedly the evidence is
words.tutor: Admittedly concedes before you argue. Say it, then say however.

words.meaning: It can be argued that; possibly.
words.example: It is arguably the better option.
practice: Arguably, that is the wrong question.
words.starter: It is arguably the better
words.tutor: Arguably softens a claim without abandoning it. Say a strong claim with and without it.

words.meaning: In fact; used to strengthen or confirm.
words.example: The cost is high — indeed, it has doubled.
practice: Indeed, that is the whole problem.
words.starter: The cost is high — indeed, it has
words.tutor: Indeed strengthens what you just said. Say a claim, then a stronger version with indeed.

words.meaning: In particular; worth mentioning specially.
words.example: Two sites failed, notably the largest.
practice: Several people objected, notably the manager.
Notably, the cost was not mentioned.
words.starter: Two sites failed, notably the
words.tutor: Notably picks out one example from several. Say a general claim then a notable case.

words.meaning: Especially; more than the others.
words.example: It is expensive, particularly for a small site.
words.starter: It is expensive, particularly for a small
words.tutor: Say not particularly. It is a very common soft negative.

readings.title: The Movement Test
readings.passage:
The most common punctuation error in English writing is not an apostrophe. It is this:
It was raining, however we went.
That is wrong, and it is wrong constantly, in work emails and reports written by people whose first language is English. The error is called a comma splice, and it happens because however feels like but.
It is not like but. However is an adverb; but is a conjunction. Conjunctions join clauses. Adverbs do not.
The correct versions are:
It was raining. However, we went.
It was raining; however, we went.
It was raining, but we went.
Rather than memorising which words belong to which class, there is a test that decides it in a second.
Can the word move inside its clause?
However, we went. We, however, went. We went, however. All three are fine, because adverbs move around.
Now try but. But we went. We but went. We went but. Only the first works, because a conjunction is fixed at the join between the clauses.
So the rule is:
If the word can move, it is an adverb. It needs a full stop or a semicolon before it.
If the word cannot move, it is a conjunction. A comma is fine.
Try it on therefore, moreover, nevertheless, consequently, furthermore. All of them move, so all of them need a full stop or a semicolon before them.
Try it on because, although, while, whereas, since, unless. None of them move, so all of them can follow a comma.
The test never fails, and it works on connectors you have not been taught.

readings.title: One Relationship, One Connector
readings.passage:
There is an error that is invisible to many learners because it feels like emphasis rather than duplication.
Although it was raining, but we went.
Both although and but express contrast, so the relationship has been marked twice. English marks it once, and the second connector has nothing to do.
This is the same error as the one Level 1 Unit 13 warned about with because and so — because it was raining, so we stayed at home. One connector or the other, never both.
The pattern generalises. In English, one relationship takes one connector, and the sentence should contain no more marking than the relationship needs.
Watch for these pairs, all of which are wrong together: although and but, because and so, despite and but, even though and however.
There is a second and subtler version of the same problem, and it is worth more attention because it survives into quite advanced writing.
A connector should mark a relationship that is actually there.
Compare these two paragraphs.
The cost is high. Furthermore, the deadline is short. Moreover, the site is difficult. Additionally, staff are stretched.
The cost is high, the deadline is short, the site is difficult, and staff are stretched.
The first looks more connected and is not. Four items in a list have been given three different connectors, none of which does anything except announce that another item is coming. The reader learns nothing from furthermore that they would not have learned from a comma.
Connectors earn their place when the relationship is not obvious without them. However earns its place because contrast might be missed. Therefore earns its place because a causal link might be missed. Furthermore, in a plain list, earns nothing.
The test is worth applying to your own writing: remove the connector and see whether the reader would still understand the relationship. If they would, the connector was decoration.

readings.title: Underconnected, Overconnected, Connected
readings.setting: The same recommendation, drafted three times by the same person.
readings.passage:
VERSION A - no connectors

  The current system is twelve years old.
  It fails about twice a month. Each
  failure costs about four hours. The
  replacement would cost 40,000. We have
  no budget this year. The failures are
  getting more frequent. I recommend we
  budget for replacement next year.

-----------------------------------------

  VERSION B - a connector everywhere

  Firstly, the current system is twelve
  years old. Furthermore, it fails about
  twice a month. Moreover, each failure
  costs about four hours. Additionally,
  the replacement would cost 40,000.
  However, we have no budget this year.
  Nevertheless, the failures are getting
  more frequent. Therefore, I recommend
  we budget for replacement next year.

-----------------------------------------

  VERSION C

  The current system is twelve years old
  and fails about twice a month, at a
  cost of roughly four hours each time.
  Replacing it would cost 40,000, which
  we do not have this year.

  However, the failures are becoming more
  frequent. If that continues, the lost
  hours will exceed the replacement cost
  within about three years.

  I therefore recommend that we budget
  for replacement next year rather than
  waiting until the system stops
  altogether.

comprehension.a: Joining two complete sentences with a comma and an adverb such as however, as in it was raining, however we went.
comprehension.why: It is the most common punctuation error in English writing and it is made constantly by first-language writers too, which is worth knowing.

comprehension.a: Can the word move inside its clause? However can — however we went, we however went, we went however — so it is an adverb. But cannot, so it is a conjunction.
comprehension.why: It decides the punctuation in a second and it works on connectors the learner has never met.

comprehension.q: What punctuation does an adverb connector need before it?
comprehension.a: A full stop or a semicolon. A comma is only enough before a conjunction.
comprehension.why: The whole error comes down to this one distinction, and the test above is what tells you which you are holding.

comprehension.q: Why is although it was raining, but we went wrong?
comprehension.a: Because although and but both mark contrast, so the relationship has been marked twice. English marks it once.
comprehension.why: It is the same error as because and so together, and it feels like emphasis rather than duplication, which is why it survives.

comprehension.q: What is the second, subtler version of the problem?
comprehension.a: Using a connector where no real relationship exists — giving four items in a plain list three different connectors that only announce another item is coming.
comprehension.why: This survives into advanced writing because it looks like structure. The reader learns nothing from furthermore that a comma would not have told them.

comprehension.q: What test does the text give for whether a connector earns its place?
comprehension.a: Remove it and see whether the reader would still understand the relationship. If they would, it was decoration.
comprehension.why: It is applicable to the learner's own writing immediately, which is what makes it more useful than a list of correct usages.

comprehension.q: What is wrong with Version A?
comprehension.a: Nothing is joined. Seven separate facts are stated and the reader has to work out every relationship between them, including the crucial one — that rising failure frequency is what changes the answer.
comprehension.why: Version A is not ungrammatical. It fails because the connections exist in the writer's head and not on the page.

comprehension.q: What is wrong with Version B?
comprehension.a: Every sentence has a connector and most of them mark nothing. Furthermore, moreover and additionally are all doing the same job — announcing another item — in what is really a list.
comprehension.why: B looks more organised than A and communicates no better. The two genuine relationships, the contrast and the conclusion, are hidden among five decorative ones.

comprehension.q: How many connectors does Version C use, and which are they?
comprehension.a: Three — however and if in the first two paragraphs, plus therefore in the last. And and which are not counted as connectors here; the rest of the joining is done by combining facts into single sentences.
comprehension.why: C uses fewer connectors than B and is far more connected, because most of the work is done by sentence structure rather than by connector words.

comprehension.q: Version C contains a sentence the other two do not. What is it and why does it matter?
comprehension.a: The lost hours will exceed the replacement cost within about three years. It matters because it is the actual argument — it turns a list of facts into a reason to act.
comprehension.why: Neither A nor B contains any reasoning at all. The connectors in B create the appearance of argument without any argument being made, which is the sharpest lesson in the document.

grammar.title: Subordinating conjunctions
grammar.explanation: These join two clauses into one sentence. You already have because from Level 1; this card adds the rest and the one rule that stops learners doubling them.
grammar.rule:
THEY JOIN TWO CLAUSES IN ONE SENTENCE

  because, although, while, whereas,
  since, as, unless, if, when,
  after, before, until, even though

EITHER ORDER WORKS
  Although it was raining, we went.
     ^ clause first -> comma
  We went although it was raining.
     ^ clause second -> usually no comma

ONE RELATIONSHIP, ONE CONNECTOR
  Although it was raining, but we went.
  ^ WRONG. Two contrast markers.

  Same error as Level 1 Unit 13:
     Because it was raining, so we stayed.
  ^ also wrong.

  Wrong pairs to watch:
     although + but
     because + so
     despite + but
     even though + however

THEY CANNOT MOVE
  Although we went.  We although went. X
  ^ that is what makes them conjunctions,
    and why a comma is enough.
grammar.workedExample:
You have two facts: it was raining, and you went anyway.
1. The relationship is concession — one thing is true and the other happened regardless.
2. Although is the concession conjunction.
3. Put the although clause first: Although it was raining, we went. A clause in front takes a comma.
4. Or put it second: We went although it was raining. No comma needed.
5. Now check for doubling. Is there a but anywhere? There should not be. Although it was raining, but we went marks the contrast twice.
One connector, one relationship. If you find yourself adding a second, delete it — the sentence is already carrying the meaning.
grammar.mistake: Doubling the connector — although with but, because with so. It feels like emphasis and it is duplication, and it is very common among learners whose first language marks the relationship at both ends. The other error is a comma before a conjunction that comes second: we went, although it was raining is acceptable but usually unnecessary.
grammar.tip: One relationship, one connector. Clause first takes a comma.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair with a subordinating conjunction. Do not use more than one.
1. It was raining. We went.
2. The site is small. It costs more to run.
3. Nobody checked. The fault was missed.
4. The first site uses the old system. The second has moved.
5. You report it in time. The claim succeeds.
6. Now write number 1 again with the clause in the other order.
grammar.answers:
1. Although it was raining, we went.
2. Although the site is small, it costs more to run.
3. Because nobody checked, the fault was missed.
4. The first site uses the old system, whereas the second has moved.
5. Provided you report it in time, the claim succeeds. (Or: If you report it in time…)
6. We went although it was raining.
Check none of yours contains two connectors. If you wrote although … but, delete the but.
Number 4 uses whereas rather than although, because the two sites are simply different — there is no concession. Card 3 covers that distinction.
In 1 to 5 the clause comes first and takes a comma. In 6 it comes second and takes none.

grammar.title: Connective adverbs and the comma splice
grammar.explanation: However, therefore, moreover and their family are adverbs, not conjunctions. They cannot join two sentences with a comma, and doing so is the most common punctuation error in English.
grammar.rule:
THE ADVERBS
  however, therefore, moreover,
  nevertheless, consequently, furthermore,
  thus, otherwise, instead, besides,
  likewise, accordingly

THEY DO NOT JOIN CLAUSES.

  It was raining, however we went.  WRONG
     ^ comma splice

  It was raining. However, we went.  right
  It was raining; however, we went.  right
  It was raining, but we went.       right

THE MOVEMENT TEST
  can the word move inside its clause?

  However, we went.
  We, however, went.
  We went, however.        all fine -> ADVERB

  But we went.
  We but went.   X
  We went but.   X        fixed -> CONJUNCTION

THE RULE
  MOVES     -> needs . or ;  before it
  DOESN'T   -> a comma is enough

The test works on connectors you have
never been taught.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write: it was raining, and you went anyway, using however.
1. First check what however is. Apply the movement test: however, we went; we, however, went; we went, however. All three work.
2. It moves, so it is an adverb.
3. Adverbs cannot join two sentences with a comma.
4. So use a full stop: It was raining. However, we went.
5. Or a semicolon: It was raining; however, we went.
Now the same idea with but.
1. Movement test: but we went works; we but went does not.
2. It is fixed, so it is a conjunction.
3. A comma is enough: It was raining, but we went.
Same meaning, three correct punctuations, and the test told you which was available in each case.
grammar.mistake: The comma splice — joining two complete sentences with a comma plus however, therefore or moreover. It is extremely common and it is made by first-language writers constantly, so it is not a learner error as such; it is simply an error. The other mistake is over-correcting into semicolons everywhere, when a full stop is usually cleaner.
grammar.tip: If it moves, it is an adverb. Full stop or semicolon before it.
grammar.practice:
Punctuate each one correctly. Some are already right.
1. It was raining however we went.
2. It was raining but we went.
3. The cost is high therefore we should wait.
4. The cost is high so we should wait.
5. It is expensive nevertheless it is the best option.
6. Although it is expensive it is the best option.
7. Nothing was recorded consequently nobody knew.
8. Nothing was recorded because nobody asked.
grammar.answers:
1. It was raining. However, we went. (or ; however,)
2. It was raining, but we went. — already correct with a comma
3. The cost is high. Therefore, we should wait. (or ; therefore,)
4. The cost is high, so we should wait. — a comma is enough
5. It is expensive. Nonetheless, it is the best option. (or ; nevertheless,)
6. Although it is expensive, it is the best option. — a comma is enough
7. Nothing was recorded. Consequently, nobody knew. (or ; consequently,)
8. Nothing was recorded because nobody asked. — no comma needed at all
The odd numbers all use adverbs and all need a full stop or semicolon. The even numbers all use conjunctions and a comma is enough.
Apply the movement test to any you got wrong. However, therefore, nevertheless and consequently all move. But, so, although and because do not.

grammar.title: Although, while and whereas
grammar.explanation: Three conjunctions that look interchangeable and are not. The difference is between conceding a point and comparing two things, and one of the three is ambiguous.
grammar.rule:
ALTHOUGH = CONCESSION
  this is true, and the other thing
  happened anyway.
     Although it was raining, we went.
     Although the site is small, it
     costs more to run.
  ^ something surprising here.

WHEREAS = COMPARISON
  two things side by side. No surprise.
     The first site uses the old system,
     whereas the second has moved.
  ^ just different. Nothing conceded.

WHILE = BOTH, plus TIME
  While it was raining, we went. concession
  ...uses the old system, while the
     second has moved.           comparison
  While I was waiting, it rained.     time
  ^ ambiguous. That is the problem.

RECOMMENDATION (style, not rule)
  although -> concession
  whereas  -> comparison
  while    -> time

DESPITE takes a NOUN, not a clause
  Despite the rain, we went.
  NOT despite it was raining.
grammar.workedExample:
You have two sites: one uses the old system and one has moved to the new one.
1. Is either fact surprising given the other? No. They are simply different.
2. Comparison takes whereas.
3. The first site uses the old system, whereas the second has moved.
4. Check by trying although: although the first site uses the old system, the second has moved. That now implies something surprising, which is not what you meant.
Now a concession. It was raining and you went anyway.
1. Is the second fact surprising given the first? Yes — rain is a reason not to go.
2. Concession takes although.
3. Although it was raining, we went.
And despite, which takes a noun: Despite the rain, we went. If you want a clause you must write despite the fact that it was raining, which is correct and heavy — so switch to although instead.
grammar.mistake: Using despite with a clause — despite it was raining. Despite is a preposition and needs a noun. The other error is using although where whereas belongs, which quietly tells the reader that one of two ordinary differences is surprising. And while for everything, which is understood but ambiguous — in careful writing it is worth reserving for time.
grammar.tip: Although concedes. Whereas compares. Despite takes a noun.
grammar.practice:
Choose although, whereas or despite.
1. ____ it was raining, we went.
2. The first site uses the old system, ____ the second has moved.
3. ____ the rain, we went.
4. ____ the site is small, it costs more to run.
5. Costs rose in the north, ____ they fell in the south.
6. ____ the cost, it is the best option.
grammar.answers:
1. Although — concession; rain is a reason not to go.
2. whereas — comparison; two sites, simply different.
3. Despite — followed by a noun, the rain.
4. Although — concession; small usually means cheaper, so this is surprising.
5. whereas — comparison; north and south side by side.
6. Despite — followed by a noun, the cost.
Numbers 3 and 6 are the despite ones and both are followed by nouns. If you wrote despite it was raining, that is the preposition taking a clause, which it cannot.
Numbers 2 and 5 are comparisons with nothing surprising in them. Try although in either and notice that it wrongly implies a contrast between the two facts.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Join without doubling
speaking.instructions:
Take ten pairs of facts from your own work or week.
Join each pair with a single subordinating conjunction — although, because, whereas, since, unless, provided.
Record all ten.
Play back and listen for a second connector. Although … but is the error, and it is very hard to hear in your own speech, which is why the recording matters.
speaking.tutor: Say ten joined sentences and ask the tutor to flag any with two connectors doing the same job.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The movement test aloud
speaking.instructions:
Take six connectors: however, therefore, moreover, but, so, although.
For each, say the same short sentence three ways — with the connector at the front, in the middle, and at the end.
However, we went. We, however, went. We went, however.
But we went. We but went. We went but.
Record all eighteen.
The ones that worked in all three positions are adverbs and need a full stop before them. The ones that only worked at the front are conjunctions.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to name six connectors and sort each into adverb or conjunction using the movement test.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Concede or compare
speaking.instructions:
Take six pairs of facts.
For each, decide whether the relationship is concession or comparison, then say it aloud with although or whereas.
Say the decision out loud first: this is a comparison, so whereas.
Record all six with their decisions.
Then say two of them the other way round and notice what changes. Although between two ordinary differences makes one of them sound surprising.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences and ask the tutor whether each one concedes something or just compares.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Two minutes, one point
speaking.instructions:
Argue one point you actually hold, for two minutes.
Use firstly and lastly to open and close.
Use at least one concession with although or admittedly, followed by however or nevertheless.
Use therefore or consequently once, for the conclusion only.
Record it.
Then listen back and count your connectors. If you used more than six in two minutes, some of them were decorating rather than connecting.
speaking.tutor: Argue a point to the tutor and ask which connectors it thought were doing real work.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Concede then continue
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these frames five times, filling them with real content.
Admittedly … However, …
Although …, …
It is true that … Nevertheless, …
I accept that … Nonetheless, …
Record the last two frames.
This shape — concede first, then argue — is the single most useful structure in this unit, because it makes a disagreement sound considered rather than reflexive.
speaking.tutor: State a position to the tutor and ask it to concede one point before disagreeing with you.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the three versions aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read all three versions aloud.
Then say aloud: what is missing from Version A, and what is wrong with Version B given that it has more connectors.
Then count the connectors in Version C and say how it joins its ideas instead.
Then say which sentence appears in C and in neither of the others, and why it changes the document.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor Version B and ask what the actual argument is.

writing.title: Writing 1 — One recommendation, three versions
writing.prompt:
Choose something you would genuinely recommend changing — at work, in a place you use, in a process you know.
Write it three times, as in Reading 3.
Version A: six to eight short sentences, no connectors at all.
Version B: the same content with a connector on every sentence.
Version C: your real version, using no more than four connectors, joining ideas by sentence structure instead, and containing at least one sentence of actual reasoning that A and B lack.
Then write two lines saying what C contains that the others do not.
writing.model:
Version C only, since A and B are exercises in doing it badly:
The kitchen has one working oven for a site that now serves ninety covers a night, up from about fifty when the second oven failed. Replacing it would cost around 3,000, which is not in this year's budget.
However, we are turning away bookings on Fridays and Saturdays, and have been since March. At roughly eight covers a night lost across two nights, the revenue foregone is already more than the cost of the oven.
I therefore recommend replacing it now from the maintenance contingency rather than waiting for next year's budget, and I have attached the two quotations.

1. C contains the calculation — eight covers times two nights against 3,000 — which is the actual argument. A and B state the facts and never connect them into a reason.
2. C uses three connectors where B used seven, and it is more connected, because most of the joining is done by putting related facts in the same sentence.
writing.criteria: Version A has no connectors; version B has one per sentence; version C uses no more than four and contains at least one sentence of reasoning absent from the others; two lines identifying what C adds; the same content in all three
writing.support: Write C first. Writing A and B afterwards is much easier than trying to write badly on purpose from a blank page, and it shows you exactly which connectors you were about to waste.
writing.extension: Delete the reasoning sentence from C and read it again. It becomes Version A with better punctuation, which is the point.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Fix the punctuation
writing.prompt:
Write twelve pairs of sentences about anything real.
Join each pair using a different connector — six adverbs and six conjunctions.
Punctuate each correctly.
Then, beside each one, write ADVERB or CONJUNCTION and show the movement test result that proved it.
writing.model:
1. The system is old. However, it works. — ADVERB (it, however, works / it works, however)
2. The system is old, but it works. — CONJUNCTION (fixed at the join)
3. Nothing was recorded. Consequently, nobody knew. — ADVERB (nobody, consequently, knew)
4. Nothing was recorded, so nobody knew. — CONJUNCTION
5. The cost is high; nevertheless, it is worth doing. — ADVERB (it is, nevertheless, worth doing)
6. Although the cost is high, it is worth doing. — CONJUNCTION
7. The site is small. Moreover, it is difficult to reach. — ADVERB
8. The site is small and it is difficult to reach. — CONJUNCTION
9. We have no budget. Therefore, we are waiting. — ADVERB
10. We are waiting because we have no budget. — CONJUNCTION
11. The first site moved; conversely, the second did not. — ADVERB
12. The first site moved, whereas the second did not. — CONJUNCTION
writing.criteria: Six adverbs and six conjunctions; every adverb preceded by a full stop or semicolon; every conjunction with a comma or none; the movement test shown for each; no pair containing two connectors
writing.support: Write the pairs in twos — the same content once with an adverb and once with a conjunction, as the model does. Seeing the same idea punctuated two ways is what fixes the rule.
writing.extension: Go back through anything you have written recently and look for a comma splice. Almost everybody finds one.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the three versions
writing.prompt:
Use the three versions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Version A is grammatically correct. Why does it fail?
2. Version B has eight connectors. Why is it not better connected than C?
3. How does Version C join its ideas, if not with connectors?
4. Which sentence appears in C alone, and what does it do?
5. Which of B's connectors would survive into a good version, and why those?
writing.model:
1. Because none of the relationships between the seven facts is on the page. The reader has to work out for themselves that rising failure frequency is what makes waiting the wrong choice, and most readers will not.
2. Because most of B's connectors mark nothing. Furthermore, moreover and additionally all announce that another item is coming, which a comma would have done. The two genuine relationships — the contrast and the conclusion — are hidden among five decorative ones.
3. Mostly by sentence structure: it combines related facts into single sentences with and, which and a relative clause, so the connection is carried by the grammar rather than announced by a word.
4. The lost hours will exceed the replacement cost within about three years. It converts a list of facts into a reason to act, and neither A nor B contains any reasoning at all.
5. However and therefore. However marks a genuine contrast — no budget against worsening failures — and therefore marks a genuine conclusion drawn from a calculation. The other six mark relationships that do not exist.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 identifies that connector count and connectedness are different things; answer 3 names sentence structure rather than word choice; answer 5 names exactly two and justifies both
writing.support: Count the facts in each version. All three have the same seven. Then count the sentences: A has seven, B has eight, C has five. The compression in C is where the connection happens.
writing.extension: Add a fourth version that keeps C's argument but removes however and therefore. Is anything lost?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. It was raining, however we went.
2. The cost is high, therefore we should wait.
3. Nothing was recorded, consequently nobody knew.
4. It is expensive, nevertheless it is the best option.
5. Although it was raining, but we went.
6. Because it was raining, so we stayed at home.
7. Despite it was raining, we went.
8. Even though it is expensive, however it is worth it.
9. The first site uses the old system, although the second has moved. (they are simply different)
10. Although the site is small, whereas it costs more to run. 
11. The system is old. Furthermore, it fails twice a month. Moreover, each failure costs four hours. Additionally, staff are stretched. (this is a plain list)
12. Firstly, the cost is high. (and there is no secondly anywhere in the document)
writing.model:
1. It was raining. However, we went. (Pattern 2 — however is an adverb and cannot follow a comma)
2. The cost is high. Therefore, we should wait. (Pattern 2 — same rule)
3. Nothing was recorded. Consequently, nobody knew. (Pattern 2 — same rule)
4. It is expensive. Nevertheless, it is the best option. (Pattern 2 — same rule)
5. Although it was raining, we went. (Pattern 1 — one relationship, one connector)
6. Because it was raining, we stayed at home. (Pattern 1 — same rule)
7. Despite the rain, we went. (Pattern 3 — despite takes a noun)
8. Even though it is expensive, it is worth it. (Pattern 1 — even though and however both mark contrast)
9. The first site uses the old system, whereas the second has moved. (Pattern 3 — comparison takes whereas)
10. Although the site is small, it costs more to run. (Pattern 1 — two connectors for one relationship)
11. The system is old and fails twice a month, at a cost of about four hours each time, and staff are stretched. (Pattern 2 — a plain list does not need three connectors)
12. The cost is high. (Pattern 2 — firstly promises a secondly that never comes)
writing.criteria: All twelve corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 1 to 4 all fixed the same way; numbers 11 and 12 fixed by deleting connectors rather than repunctuating
writing.support: Numbers 1 to 4 are one error four times. Apply the movement test to each connector, confirm it is an adverb, and replace the comma with a full stop. Do all four before moving on.
writing.extension: Numbers 11 and 12 were correctly punctuated and still wrong. Write two more like them.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Join with one connector
activities.instructions:
Join each pair with a single subordinating conjunction. Never use two.
1. It was raining. We went.
2. The site is small. It costs more to run.
3. Nobody checked. The fault was missed.
4. The first site uses the old system. The second has moved.
5. You report it in time. The claim succeeds.
6. The evidence is thin. The conclusion may be right.
7. Costs rose in the north. They fell in the south.
8. The part had not arrived. The engineer could not finish.
9. It is expensive. It is the best option.
10. Nothing changes. We will finish on Friday.
11. He qualified in 2018. He had no experience before that.
12. The system is twelve years old. It still works.
activities.answers:
1. Although it was raining, we went.
2. Although the site is small, it costs more to run.
3. Because nobody checked, the fault was missed.
4. The first site uses the old system, whereas the second has moved.
5. Provided you report it in time, the claim succeeds.
6. Although the evidence is thin, the conclusion may be right.
7. Costs rose in the north, whereas they fell in the south.
8. Because the part had not arrived, the engineer could not finish.
9. Although it is expensive, it is the best option.
10. Unless something changes, we will finish on Friday.
11. He qualified in 2018, although he had no experience before that.
12. Although the system is twelve years old, it still works.
Check none of yours contains two connectors doing the same job.
Numbers 4 and 7 are comparisons and take whereas — nothing about either fact is surprising given the other. Everything else marked with although has something genuinely surprising in it.
Number 10 uses unless, and notice the verb after it is positive: something changes, not nothing changes.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Adverb or conjunction?
activities.instructions:
Punctuate each correctly, then write ADVERB or CONJUNCTION.
1. It was raining however we went.
2. It was raining but we went.
3. The cost is high therefore we should wait.
4. The cost is high so we should wait.
5. It is expensive nevertheless it is the best option.
6. Although it is expensive it is the best option.
7. Nothing was recorded consequently nobody knew.
8. Nothing was recorded because nobody asked.
9. The site is small moreover it is hard to reach.
10. The site is small and it is hard to reach.
11. The first moved conversely the second did not.
12. The first moved whereas the second did not.
13. We have no budget thus nothing was done.
14. We have no budget so nothing was done.
15. It failed twice furthermore it was never checked.
16. It failed twice since it was never checked.
activities.answers:
Odd numbers are all ADVERBS and need a full stop or semicolon. Even numbers are all CONJUNCTIONS and take a comma or nothing.
1. It was raining. However, we went. — ADVERB
2. It was raining, but we went. — CONJUNCTION
3. The cost is high. Therefore, we should wait. — ADVERB
4. The cost is high, so we should wait. — CONJUNCTION
5. It is expensive. Nevertheless, it is the best option. — ADVERB
6. Although it is expensive, it is the best option. — CONJUNCTION
7. Nothing was recorded. Consequently, nobody knew. — ADVERB
8. Nothing was recorded because nobody asked. — CONJUNCTION
9. The site is small. Moreover, it is hard to reach. — ADVERB
10. The site is small and it is hard to reach. — CONJUNCTION
11. The first moved; conversely, the second did not. — ADVERB
12. The first moved, whereas the second did not. — CONJUNCTION
13. We have no budget. Thus nothing was done. — ADVERB
14. We have no budget, so nothing was done. — CONJUNCTION
15. It failed twice. Furthermore, it was never checked. — ADVERB
16. It failed twice since it was never checked. — CONJUNCTION
Apply the movement test to any you got wrong. However, therefore, nevertheless, consequently, moreover, conversely, thus and furthermore all move inside their clause. But, so, although, because, and, whereas and since do not.
Number 13 shows thus often taking no comma, which is a stylistic difference rather than a rule.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Although, whereas or despite?
activities.instructions:
Choose although, whereas or despite.
1. ____ it was raining, we went.
2. The first site uses the old system, ____ the second has moved.
3. ____ the rain, we went.
4. ____ the site is small, it costs more to run.
5. Costs rose in the north, ____ they fell in the south.
6. ____ the cost, it is the best option.
7. ____ the evidence is thin, the conclusion may be right.
8. Demand rose in March, ____ it fell in April.
9. ____ the delay, we finished on time.
10. ____ nobody checked it, the fault was found.
11. The old machines are reliable, ____ the new ones are not.
12. ____ everything, it worked.
activities.answers:
1. Although  2. whereas  3. Despite  4. Although  5. whereas  6. Despite  7. Although  8. whereas  9. Despite  10. Although  11. whereas  12. Despite
The four despite items — 3, 6, 9 and 12 — are all followed by nouns: the rain, the cost, the delay, everything. Despite cannot take a clause.
The four whereas items — 2, 5, 8 and 11 — are all plain comparisons. Nothing in either half is surprising given the other. Try although in any of them and it wrongly implies a contrast.
The four although items all contain something genuinely surprising: going out in the rain, a small site costing more, thin evidence supporting a right answer, a fault being found without checking.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Does the connector earn its place?
activities.instructions:
For each sentence pair, write EARNS or DECORATION. Then rewrite the DECORATION ones without the connector.
1. The cost is high. However, it is the only option.
2. The cost is high. Furthermore, the deadline is short.
3. Nothing was recorded. Therefore, nobody knew.
4. The site is small. Additionally, it is dark.
5. It failed twice. Nevertheless, nobody replaced it.
6. We have three suppliers. Moreover, we have two warehouses.
7. The evidence is thin. Consequently, the conclusion is uncertain.
8. There are four staff. Likewise, there are four vans.
activities.answers:
EARNS: 1, 3, 5, 7.
DECORATION: 2, 4, 6, 8.
2. The cost is high and the deadline is short.
4. The site is small and dark.
6. We have three suppliers and two warehouses.
8. There are four staff and four vans.
The four that earn their place all mark a relationship the reader could miss: a contrast in 1 and 5, and a causal link in 3 and 7. Remove the connector from any of them and the reader has to work out the relationship themselves.
The four that do not are all plain lists. Furthermore, additionally, moreover and likewise are announcing that another item is coming, which is what and does, in one syllable.
Number 8 is worth noticing. Likewise implies a meaningful parallel between the two facts, and there is none — it is a coincidence of numbers.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Audit your own writing
activities.instructions:
Find something you have written in the last month — an email, a message, a report, an application.
Mark every connector.
For each, write EARNS or DECORATION using the test from Reading 2: remove it and see whether the relationship is still clear.
Then check every adverb connector for a comma splice.
Rewrite one paragraph.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your writing.
What most people find: fewer connectors than they expected, and at least one comma splice. The splice is almost always with however, and it is almost always in a sentence the writer thought was one of their better ones.
The second finding is about distribution. Connectors cluster at the start of paragraphs, where writers feel the need to signal a transition, and disappear inside paragraphs where the real relationships are. That is the wrong way round — a reader can usually see a paragraph break, and cannot see an unmarked contrast in the middle of one.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Count them in real prose
activities.instructions:
Take one page of real written English — a news article, a report, a set of instructions, an official letter.
Count the connectors on the page and note which ones appear.
Then count how many sentences have no connector at all.
Then find one comma splice, if there is one.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: far fewer connectors than they expected. A well-written page often has three or four, and most sentences have none — the relationships are carried by the order of the ideas and by sentence structure.
The second finding depends on what you chose. Academic and official writing uses more of them, and uses the formal ones — thus, hence, accordingly, notwithstanding. Journalism uses very few and relies on however almost exclusively.
The third finding is the interesting one. Comma splices appear in published, edited English regularly, particularly with however. That does not make them correct, and it is worth knowing that the error you are learning to avoid is one that professional writers make too.

options: It was raining, however we went.
It was raining however, we went.
It was raining. However, we went.
It was raining, however, we went.
quizzes.a: It was raining. However, we went.
quizzes.why: However is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two sentences with a comma. A full stop or a semicolon is needed.

options: Whether the word is formal
Whether the sentence can be reversed
Whether the word has more than two syllables
Whether the word can move inside its clause
quizzes.a: Whether the word can move inside its clause
quizzes.why: However moves — however we went, we however went, we went however — so it is an adverb. But is fixed at the join, so it is a conjunction.

options: The cost is high, so we should wait.
The cost is high, therefore we should wait.
The cost is high therefore, we should wait.
The cost is high therefore we should wait.
quizzes.a: The cost is high, so we should wait.
quizzes.why: So is a conjunction and a comma is enough. Therefore is an adverb and would need a full stop or semicolon before it.

options: Although it was raining, we went.
Although it was raining, but we went.
It was raining, but we went.
Despite the rain, we went.
quizzes.a: Although it was raining, but we went.
quizzes.why: Although and but both mark contrast, so the relationship is marked twice. English marks it once — the same error as because and so together.

options: Despite it was raining, we went.
Despite of the rain, we went.
Despite the rain, we went.
Despite that it was raining, we went.
quizzes.why: Despite is a preposition and takes a noun. For a clause you would need despite the fact that, which is correct and heavy — switch to although instead.

quizzes.q: The first site uses the old system, ____ the second has moved. Which fits?
options: although
however
despite
whereas
quizzes.why: This is a comparison — two sites, simply different, with nothing surprising about either. Although would wrongly imply a concession.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between although and whereas?
options: Although concedes; whereas compares
Although is more formal
Whereas is only used in writing
There is no difference
quizzes.why: Although means this is true and the other thing happened anyway. Whereas sets two things side by side with no surprise involved.

quizzes.q: Reading 2 says a connector should mark a relationship that is actually there. What is the test?
options: Count the syllables
Remove it and see whether the relationship is still clear
Check whether it is formal enough
Check whether it appears at the start of the sentence
quizzes.a: Remove it and see whether the relationship is still clear
quizzes.why: If the reader would understand it anyway, the connector was decoration. Furthermore in a plain list tells the reader nothing that a comma would not.

quizzes.q: Version B of the recommendation has eight connectors. Why is it not well connected?
options: The connectors are too formal
It has too few sentences
Most of them mark relationships that do not exist
The connectors are wrongly punctuated
quizzes.a: Most of them mark relationships that do not exist
quizzes.why: Furthermore, moreover and additionally all just announce another item in what is really a list. The two genuine relationships are hidden among five decorative ones.

quizzes.q: How does Version C join its ideas?
options: With more connectors than B
With semicolons throughout
By using shorter sentences
Mostly by combining related facts into single sentences
quizzes.a: Mostly by combining related facts into single sentences
quizzes.why: C uses three connectors to B's eight and is far more connected, because the joining is done by grammar rather than announced by connector words.

quizzes.q: Which of these needs a full stop or semicolon before it?
options: nevertheless
although
whereas
because
quizzes.why: Nevertheless moves inside its clause, so it is an adverb. The other three are conjunctions, fixed at the join, and a comma is enough.

quizzes.q: Firstly, the cost is high — and the document never says secondly. What is wrong?
options: Firstly is too formal
Firstly promises a sequence that never arrives
Firstly should be first
Nothing is wrong
quizzes.a: Firstly promises a sequence that never arrives
quizzes.why: The sentence is correctly punctuated and still wrong, because the connector makes a commitment to the reader that the writing does not keep.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it is built as eight pairs — the same relationship expressed once with an adverb and once with a conjunction — so the punctuation rule emerges from the learner's own answers.

teacherNotes.type: Organise by attachment, not by meaning
teacherNotes.note: Learners can already understand these words when reading; what they cannot do is punctuate them. Grouping by grammatical class rather than by meaning is what makes the unit teachable, and the movement test is the whole of it. The test works on connectors that have not been taught, which is why it is worth more than any list.

teacherNotes.type: The comma splice is not a learner error
teacherNotes.note: It is made constantly in edited, published English, particularly with however, and Practice 6 asks learners to find one in real prose. Saying this plainly prevents the demoralising experience of learning a rule and then seeing it broken everywhere. The rule is still worth following; the learner simply needs to know that seeing it broken is not evidence they misunderstood.

Although with but, and because with so, are extremely common among learners whose first language marks a relationship at both ends, and they do not feel like errors — they feel like reinforcement. Naming the pattern as one relationship, one connector, and linking it back to the Level 1 Unit 13 warning, is more effective than treating each pair separately.

teacherNotes.type: The decoration problem is the harder half
teacherNotes.note: Correct punctuation with connectors that mark nothing produces Version B, which looks organised and communicates no better than Version A. Practice 4 and the removal test address this directly. It is worth spending as much time here as on the punctuation, because it survives much longer — learners fix the comma splice and then write furthermore for years.

teacherNotes.type: Why three versions of one paragraph
teacherNotes.note: Version A is underconnected, B is overconnected, and C is connected. The decisive point is that C contains a sentence of reasoning that neither of the others has: the connectors in B create the appearance of argument without any argument being made. Writing 1 asks learners to produce all three of their own, and the support note tells them to write C first, because writing badly on purpose from a blank page is harder than degrading something good.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 asks learners to audit their own recent writing, which may include work emails, applications or personal messages: none of that text should be collected, shared or entered into the app, and the task asks only for connector counts and a rewritten paragraph the learner keeps. Practice 6 uses published material, which carries no such concern. Writing 1 asks for a recommendation about a real workplace — learners should avoid naming employers or colleagues.

selfAssessment.statement: I can join two clauses with although or whereas and not add but as well.
I can tell a comma splice from a correct sentence, and fix it.
I can use although for concession and whereas for comparison and know which I mean.
I can tell whether a paragraph is connected or just punctuated to look connected.

assignment.title: One recommendation, three ways
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record two minutes arguing one point you actually hold, opening with firstly, conceding once with although or admittedly followed by however, and concluding with therefore — then listen back, count your connectors, and record one sentence naming any that were decorating rather than connecting. Second, write the same recommendation three times as directed in Writing 1, with no connectors, then one per sentence, then your real version using no more than four and containing a sentence of actual reasoning; add the twelve punctuated pairs from Writing 2 with the movement test shown for each, and your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3. Keep everything together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written work
